scenario.speaker: marcus
scenario.briefing:
We won it. Dana signed the **Neo Smart Living** engagement this morning — secondary research, focus groups, and a survey over fourteen weeks. It's the largest project on the board, and phase one starts with you.

Phase one is **secondary research**. Neo needs to know three things before we spend a dollar on primary data: who the Tahoe Mini actually competes against, which features the market is rewarding, and where the price benchmarks sit. I've pulled three recent industry articles — they're attached to my memo in your **Inbox**, and they contain everything you need if you read them like an analyst instead of like a magazine subscriber.

Your three assignments: identify the **competitive set**, recommend the **feature priorities**, and extract the **price benchmarks** for the compact, standard, and deluxe formats. The **Guides** button has my method for pulling findings out of secondary sources without drowning in them. Extraction, not summary — Dana reads the output of this round in Friday's client call.

inbox.subject: We got Neo — phase one is yours
inbox.body:
First things first: your proposal work paid off. Neo Smart Living signed this morning — all three phases, fourteen weeks. Dana actually smiled in a meeting, which the old-timers tell me happens once a fiscal year.

Now the bill comes due. Phase one is secondary research, and the client call is Friday, so we move today. I've pulled three industry articles covering the compact backyard-structure category — they're attached below. Together they hold the answers to the three questions Neo is paying us for this phase:

1. **Competitive set.** Seven companies show up in the category coverage. Only some of them are true competitors to a $23,000 finished backyard studio. Work out which three belong on Neo's benchmark list.
2. **Feature priorities.** The buyer-trends and forecast pieces tell you what the market rewards and what it punishes. Turn that into a recommended specification, category by category.
3. **Price benchmarks.** The competitive-outlook piece has every price point you need. Derive the mid-market benchmark for the compact, standard, and deluxe formats — that's the ruler we'll hold the Tahoe Mini against all project long.

Read all three articles before you answer anything; they check each other. And keep your tiers straight — averaging a luxury sauna into a mid-market benchmark is the kind of mistake that follows an analyst around.

— Marcus

attachments.title: Competitive Outlook on Compact Backyard Structures in North America
attachments.body:
*Structure & Site Quarterly — annual category review*

The North American market for compact accessory structures — factory-built backyard studios, offices, and shed-adjacent units sold finished or as kits — posted another year of growth, and the field has now sorted itself into four recognizable tiers: a crowded mid-market, a permitted-ADU tier above it, a luxury fringe, and a budget basement. Buyers increasingly shop within a tier rather than across them, which makes tier discipline the first rule of any competitive read.

**The mid-market is where the volume is.** StudioPod Co. remains the tier's revenue leader at an estimated $19 million annually. The company built its position on quick installation, pre-wired electrical, and modern glazing, and prices its three-format lineup at $12,000 (compact), $18,000 (standard), and $24,000 (deluxe). YardHaus, at an estimated $14 million, undercuts the leader slightly — $11,500 / $17,500 / $23,500 across the same formats — behind modular panels and a DIY-friendly assembly story. ModuSpace, estimated at $11 million, prices at a premium to both ($13,000 / $18,500 / $25,000) and earns it with a standard climate package and office fit-out options.

**Above the mid-market**, Casita Collective (est. $8 million) is often mis-shelved with this category: its units are permitted accessory dwelling units with plumbing, priced at $28,000 / $42,000 / $60,000 — a different regulatory and cost structure entirely, sold as a construction project rather than a delivered product. On the luxury fringe, Tropez Outdoor (est. $3 million) sells backyard spa and sauna units at $35,000 / $48,000 / $70,000 to a small resort-at-home clientele.

**Below**, ZenShed (est. $6 million) moves kit shells with no electrical at $6,500 / $9,000 / $12,500, and BackyardBox (est. $4 million) sells storage-grade, unfinished units at $5,500 / $8,500 / $11,000. Both compete on price against each other, not on finished, occupiable space.

Format sizes have quietly standardized across the tiers: compact runs roughly 100 square feet, standard roughly 120, and deluxe roughly 160. Category analysts peg the mid-market sweet spot at $12,000 / $18,000 / $24,000 for compact, standard, and deluxe formats — the ladder against which any new entrant's pricing will be measured. Entrants who priced above that ladder without permitted square footage have struggled to hold share past their first two selling seasons.

attachments.title: Backyard-Unit Buyer Trends by Homeowner Segment
attachments.body:
*Home & Yard Business Journal — buyer-trends brief*

Who actually buys a finished backyard unit, and what do they want from it once it lands? Retailer interviews and two waves of syndicated purchase-tracking data point to three homeowner segments with distinct — and occasionally conflicting — demands.

**The remote professional** accounts for roughly forty-five percent of tracked purchases, and this buyer wants an office, not a room. Purchase drivers are consistent: separation from the household, daylight ("I refuse to work in a garage cave," one buyer told our researchers), and a desk-ready interior — work surface, shelving, task lighting — rather than an empty shell they must furnish themselves. Yet the same glass-forward designs that win this buyer at purchase generate the category's two most common post-purchase complaints: afternoon heat gain and the sensation of "working on display" in view of neighboring second-story windows. Demand has shifted accordingly toward dual-pane glazing with a privacy option — switchable film, integral blinds, or solid-panel swaps — rather than either fully glazed or nearly windowless designs.

**The wellness user** — roughly thirty percent of purchases and the fastest-growing segment — wants a yoga, meditation, or small-fitness studio. This buyer asks about resilient or sprung flooring, a mirror wall, air movement, and, more than any other segment, privacy. Retailers report wellness buyers walking away from all-glass showroom units after a single question: "Can the neighbors see in?"

**The guest-space buyer** rounds out the category at roughly a quarter of purchases and is softening: interest cools quickly once shoppers learn that unplumbed, non-habitable structures cannot legally or practically serve as true guest quarters.

Two demands now cut across all three segments. First, climate comfort has become a threshold expectation rather than an upgrade: buyers in the hotter inland and Sun Belt metros increasingly treat insulation plus a mini-split heating-and-cooling unit as the minimum for year-round use, and units marketed with fans-only ventilation are drawing elevated complaint and return rates. Second, buyers rarely ask about smart-home extras unprompted, but they expect the basics handled on day one: powered outlets installed by a professional and a door that locks.

attachments.title: Opportunities & Forecasts for the North American Compact-Structure Market
attachments.body:
*Compact Structures Outlook — five-year category forecast*

Forecasters expect the compact accessory-structure category to grow at roughly eleven percent annually through 2030, with the persistence of remote and hybrid work as the primary demand engine and permit-light formats — units sized under local permitting thresholds — as the primary supply-side accelerant. Growth is projected to concentrate in Sun Belt and West Coast metros, where year-round outdoor usability and high housing costs make a finished backyard room an attractive alternative to moving. The mid-market tier is projected to capture the majority of that growth; the budget tier grows in units but not much in dollars, and the permitted-ADU tier remains constrained by regulatory timelines.

**Feature outlook.** Synthesizing buyer surveys, dealer interviews, and warranty-claim data, our analysts project the five attributes buyers will most demand over the forecast window:

1. **Insulated composite panel construction** — the single strongest predictor of owner satisfaction in claims and review data
2. **Dual-pane glazing with a privacy option** — resolving the category's signature heat-and-exposure complaints without giving up daylight
3. **A full climate package** — insulation plus mini-split heating and cooling, increasingly expected as standard
4. **Work-from-home interior fit-out** — desk, shelving, and lighting delivered ready to use
5. **Pre-wired electrical with smart entry lock** — professional power on day one, with security handled quietly in the background

On materials, the same data carries warnings: single-skin steel and untreated timber kits are losing share on durability and comfort complaints, and while premium hardwood cladding tests well aesthetically, few buyers in this category will pay its increment — it wins compliments, not orders. Unfinished shells continue to disappoint owners who underestimate finishing costs.

**Pricing outlook.** Analysts expect mid-market pricing to hold flat or drift modestly downward as new entrants arrive and panel manufacturing scales; nobody projects room above the established mid-market ladder for an unpermitted structure. The consensus view: pricing above that ladder is difficult to sustain without permitted, plumbed square footage to show for it, while pricing far below it signals "shed" to a buyer shopping for a room. New entrants are advised to enter at or just below the prevailing mid-market benchmarks and compete on specification rather than on premium positioning.

groups.context: The buyer-trends article documents the category's two most common post-purchase complaints in glass-forward units, and the forecast article's feature outlook names the design that resolves both.

groups.context: The buyer-trends article describes what climate comfort has become across all three buyer segments — especially in hotter inland metros — and the forecast article's feature list confirms the direction.

groups.context: The buyer-trends article sizes the three buyer segments and states what each wants delivered ready to use; the forecast article notes how unfinished shells perform with owners. Two answers are defensible here — pick the one you would lead with.

options.label: Wellness package: sprung floor + mirror wall

groups.label: Power & security
groups.context: The forecast article's feature outlook covers power and security in one line, and the buyer-trends article explains which basics buyers expect handled on day one. The competitive-outlook article shows which power setups the tiers ship with.

tasks.prompt: From the articles, what mid-market price benchmark should Neo carry into the next research phase for each format? Enter whole dollars.

entries.context: The deluxe rung of the mid-market ladder. The competitive-outlook article gives you both the raw prices and the analysts' benchmark — they should agree closely.

guides.title: Round 4 — Reading Secondary Research Without Drowning
guides.body:
**Extraction beats summary.** A summary tells your boss what an article said; an extraction answers the client's question. Before you read a word, write down the table you intend to fill — then read only to fill it.

**Make three passes, one per question:**

1. **Competitor grid.** For every company named: revenue or size, market tier, price points, and its one-line claim to fame. Then apply the definition that matters: a *competitor* is a company your buyer would cross-shop — not every company with a backyard SKU. Sort by tier before you compare anything.
2. **Feature signals.** Collect what buyers *praise*, what they *complain about after purchase* (the strongest signal in secondary data — it's behavior, not opinion), and what forecasters *rank*. When a complaint and a forecast point at the same feature, that's your headline.
3. **Price benchmarks.** Pull every price point into one ladder, tier by tier. Averages are only meaningful *within* a tier — one luxury unit in your math can move a benchmark by thousands.

**Triangulate.** A finding in one source is a claim; the same finding in two independent sources is a finding; in three, it's a plan. When sources disagree, recency and independence break the tie.

**Check recency and credibility.** Note each piece's publication cadence and vantage point. "Est." before a revenue figure means someone modeled it, not audited it — fine for ranking companies, risky for precision claims. Trade-press analysis beats vendor-sponsored content; data with a described method beats data without one.

**Pointers for this round:** keep the four tiers separate before averaging anything; when analysts state an explicit benchmark, treat it as a hypothesis and verify it against the raw table — here they should agree closely; and read all three articles before answering, because the feature questions are answered across two of them, not one.
